content.title: About
content.content: Black bean sauce is a traditional Chinese condiment made from fermented black soybeans (douchi), salt, sugar, and sometimes aromatics such as garlic, ginger, and chili. It delivers a deep umami flavor with subtle sweet and salty notes and is commonly used in meat, seafood, and vegetable dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black bean sauce has been used in Chinese cuisine for over 2,000 years, especially in Sichuan and Guangdong cooking.
The term “douchi” (豆豉) refers to fermented soybeans, not to tofu.
Traditional fermentation can last from several months to a year, giving the sauce its distinctive aroma.
In Western kitchens the sauce is often employed as a richer alternative to regular soy sauce.
The black beans used are rich in probiotics that may support gut health.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Fermentation of black soybeans creates beneficial bacteria that can aid digestive health.

items.title: Source of protein and fiber
items.content: Black soybeans provide plant‑based protein and dietary fiber, promoting satiety and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytoestrogens and polyphenols in the sauce help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Low in saturated fat and containing isoflavones, it may benefit heart health.

items.title: Flavorful with few calories
items.content: Despite its intense taste, the sauce is low in calories, making it a good alternative to richer sauces.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Black bean sauce is typically salty, so people with hypertension should use it sparingly.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy should avoid the sauce as it can trigger reactions, including anaphylaxis.

items.title: Glutamate sensitivity
items.content: The fermented product is rich in glutamate, which may cause sensitivity in some people.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Some commercial versions contain added sugar, increasing the calorie count.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add black bean sauce to marinades, stir‑fry sauces, soups, and braised dishes. It is a key ingredient in mapo tofu, beef with black bean sauce, vegetable stir‑fries, and seafood preparations. Typically 1–2 tablespoons are enough to impart a deep savory flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in a tightly sealed jar at room temperature before opening (up to 6 months). After opening, keep it refrigerated; it will stay good for up to 12 months. Discard if mold appears or the aroma changes.

content.title: About
content.content: NFS Cookie is a sweet baked product made from flour, sugar, butter and various add‑ins such as chocolate, nuts or raisins. It features a crisp edge and a soft, aromatic interior. The snack is popular as a quick bite and is often served with tea or coffee.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mass production of cookies began in the 19th century in the United States.
There are more than 400 varieties of cookies, ranging from simple sugar cookies to complex spiced recipes.
Cookies are frequently used as a base for no‑bake desserts like cheesecake crusts.
In many cultures cookies are a traditional gift for holidays.
The term “home‑baked cookie” denotes products made without industrial additives.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates provide a quick boost of energy, making cookies a convenient snack.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Small amounts of B1 and B2 support carbohydrate metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: When whole‑grain flour or nuts are used, cookies can contribute to digestive health.

items.title: Antioxidants from add‑ins
items.content: Chocolate, dried fruit or nuts add antioxidant compounds.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Sugar triggers serotonin release, which can temporarily lift mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may lead to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Cookies often contain nuts, gluten and dairy, which can cause allergic reactions.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some commercial recipes use partially hydrogenated oils, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Cookies can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, problematic for people with diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cookies can be enjoyed on their own, paired with tea, coffee or milk, or incorporated into desserts such as layered cakes or ice‑cream mixes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: The Double Hamburger is a classic fast‑food item consisting of two small beef patties (about 85 g each), a bun, lettuce, a slice of cheese, pickles, onion and sauce. It delivers a richer meat flavor than a single patty while keeping the portion convenient.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Double hamburgers appeared on major fast‑food menus in the early 1990s as a response to consumer demand for a more "meaty" option.
Each patty weighs roughly 85 g, giving about 170 g of pure beef in total.
In some countries the double is served with double cheese, pushing the calorie count to around 600 kcal.
The bun is usually toasted with butter, creating a golden crust and a buttery aroma.
The combination of two patties and sauce makes the sandwich juicier but also raises fat and sodium levels.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Beef patties provide approximately 20 g of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Red meat is rich in heme iron and zinc, nutrients important for immune function and metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy production.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The high calorie content offers a quick energy boost, useful during periods of increased physical activity.

items.title: Fiber from the bun
items.content: When the bun is made from whole‑grain flour, it adds a modest amount of dietary fiber.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Two patties increase saturated fat intake, which may raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauce and pickles add significant salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Caloric load
items.content: A double hamburger can contain 500–700 kcal, requiring careful accounting in daily energy balance.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bun typically contains wheat, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The double hamburger is usually served in a paper wrapper. Eat it with your hands, adding extra sauce, ketchup or mustard if desired. For a healthier twist, swap the bun for a whole‑grain version or omit one slice of cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared double hamburger in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze it and reheat in an oven or microwave to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

ham-or-pork-noodles-and-vegetables-exclu.title: Ham or pork with noodles and vegetables without carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens, no sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of diced ham or lean pork, boiled wheat noodles, and a mix of vegetables such as bell pepper, zucchini and sweet corn, prepared without any sauce. It is popular in Asian and European cuisines as a quick, nutritious meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ham is often smoked, giving the dish a distinctive aroma.
Pork is a good source of vitamin B12 and zinc.
Wheat noodles provide complex carbohydrates that keep you feeling full longer.
Excluding carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens makes the dish easier on sensitive stomachs.
The whole meal can be cooked in a single pan, saving time and dishes.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ham and pork supply high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle repair.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Noodles deliver glucose, supporting sustained energy throughout the day.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pork contains thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which aid carbohydrate metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Both meats provide iron and zinc, important for immune function.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: The absence of sauce and sweet vegetables keeps the dish low in added sugars, suitable for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ham can be high in salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium varieties or use less.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Pork may contain saturated fat; opting for lean cuts reduces this risk.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat noodles contain gluten, making the dish unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Processed meat additives
items.content: Some hams contain preservatives; select products without added nitrites when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, tossing the noodles with the meat and vegetables. A drizzle of olive oil or a squeeze of lemon juice can enhance flavor. Plate in a deep bowl and garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in a pan or microwave, adding a splash of water to keep the noodles from drying out.
